extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and inventors (especially those involved in priority/interference disputes)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating conception, reduction to practice, reasonable diligence, and related obviousness/ownership issues in patent prosecution and interference/priority disputes. Covers legal standards, evidentiary requirements, and illustrative case guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception — definite and permanent idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the formation in the mind of the inventor of a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention (a disclosure enabling one skilled in the art to reduce it to practice without extensive experimentation or inventive skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception requires possession of every feature recited in the count and must be proved by corroborating evidence. Case citations: Hiatt v. Ziegler; Gunter v. Stream; Coleman v. Dines; Hybritech Inc. v. Monoclonal Antibodies Inc. Examples and notes: Conception is distinct from enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception must be in the mind of the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must form a definite and permanent idea of the complete and operable invention to establish conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony by noninventors about meaning of variables may be insufficient to establish what the inventors conceived. Case citation: Bosies v. Benedict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of others' ideas permitted if inventor maintains intellectual domination
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may adopt ideas, suggestions, and materials from others so long as the inventor maintains intellectual domination over making the invention down to successful testing, selecting or rejecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources may include employees, consultants, or friends; the inventor must retain control of the inventive process. Case citations: Morse v. Porter; Staehelin v. Secher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous recognition and appreciation required for conception
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention for conception to be established; accidental and unappreciated duplication does not defeat a properly recognized invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor need not know that the invention will work or appreciate patentability to have conception, but must have recognized the inventive subject matter at the time. Case citations: Silvestri v. Grant; Invitrogen Corp. v. Clontech; Burroughs Wellcome Co. v. Barr Labs.; Dow Chem. Co. v. Astro-Valcour. Examples explain that mere 'hope' without a definite and permanent understanding is insufficient (Hitzeman v. Rutter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of species vs genus — sufficiency requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception of a species is not necessarily conception of the genus, and conception of one species may not constitute conception of other species in the same genus; for chemicals and genes, conception requires idea of the structure and an operative method for making it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining a gene by principal biological property without details and method is insufficient; conception is not enablement. Case citations: In re Jolley; Oka v. Youssefyeh; Amgen v. Chugai; Fiers v. Revel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception may coincide with reduction to practice in unpredictable arts
rubrics_metrics.description: On rare occasions, conception and reduction to practice occur simultaneously, particularly in unpredictable areas of chemistry and biology where there is no conception until the invention is reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is not complete if subsequent experimentation undermines the specificity of the inventor's idea. Case citations: Alpert v. Slatin; MacMillan v. Moffett; Hitzeman v. Rutter; Dunn v. Ragin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned application not copending is evidence only of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A previously abandoned application with which no subsequent application was co-pending serves only as evidence of conception and does not provide constructive reduction to practice benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an original application that is later abandoned does not preserve its constructive reduction to practice benefit if not co-pending or properly referenced; the abandoned filing remains evidence of conception. Case citation: In re Costello.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction to practice requires compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on an earlier-filed U.S. patent application for constructive reduction to practice, the earlier application must satisfy the written description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for the subject matter of the count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must include all limitations of the interference count or show that absent text is necessarily comprehended; disclosure must be sufficient that the only reasonable construction by a PHOSITA supports each positive limitation. Case citations: Hyatt v. Boone; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Edwards. Note: generic terms may sometimes be sufficient for species (Bigham v. Godtfredsen) but exceptions exist when species are patentably distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice — two-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish an actual reduction to practice in an interference, a party must (1) have constructed an embodiment or performed a process that met every element of the interference count, and (2) the embodiment or process must have operated for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same evidence that proves constructive reduction may be insufficient for actual reduction; actual reduction requires physical/tangible form showing every element. Case citation: Eaton v. Evans; Wetmore v. Quick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice requires sufficient testing to demonstrate workability
rubrics_metrics.description: For an actual reduction to practice, the invention must have been sufficiently tested to demonstrate that it will work for its intended purpose, though commercial readiness is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent and character of testing varies with complexity of invention; simple devices may require little testing if purpose/efficacy are obvious. Case citations: Scott v. Finney; King Instrument Corp. v. Otari Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of testing depends on facts and relationship to intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing required to establish reduction to practice depends on the particular facts, especially the nature of the invention; tests need not duplicate all actual-use conditions if evidence establishes relationship between test conditions and intended functional setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bench/lab tests must either duplicate conditions of actual use or establish a relationship between subject matter, test conditions, and intended functional setting. Examples: Gellert v. Wanberg; Wells v. Fremont.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice requires contemporaneous recognition by inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: An experiment or embodiment constitutes a reduction to practice only if there was contemporaneous appreciation of the invention by the inventor; subsequent recognition cannot be used to establish prior reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of later testing may be used to show an embodiment was produced and met the limitations, but contemporaneous appreciation is required for dating. Case citations: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Meitzner v. Corte; Estee Lauder, Inc. v. L'Oreal S.A.; Parker v. Frilette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inurement — third-party recognition may inure to inventor under conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the invention by another may inure to the benefit of the inventor if (1) the inventor conceived the invention, (2) the inventor had an expectation the embodiment tested would work for its intended purpose, and (3) the inventor submitted the embodiment for testing for that intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any prong is missing (e.g., samples tested by non-inventor without submission for intended-purpose testing), the non-inventor's recognition will not inure. Case citation: Genentech Inc. v. Chiron Corp.; Cooper v. Goldfarb.

rubrics_metrics.name: In an interference, all limitations of a count must be reduced to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The device or embodiment reduced to practice must include every limitation of the interference count; every limitation is material and must be proved to establish an actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No doctrine of equivalents for proving reduction in interference context; remedy is motion to amend count to conform to proofs. Case citations: Fredkin v. Irasek; Meitzner v. Corte; Hull v. Bonis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known utility required at time of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known utility for the invention at the time of reduction to practice (exceptions: plant and design inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility may be established by demonstration or satisfactory correlation (including animal tests where correlations exist). Case citations: Wiesner v. Weigert; Azar v. Burns; Ciric v. Flanigen; Engelhardt v. Judd; Rey-Bellet v. Engelhardt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable utility is generally insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable utility or a strong probability of utility does not establish practical utility sufficient for reduction to practice; actual testing or utility that can be 'foretold with certainty' is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening tests indicating possible utility are insufficient. However, in cases where reasonable correlation between observed properties and suggested uses exists, evidence may be judged as a whole (Nelson v. Bowler). Case citations: Bindra v. Kelly; Wu v. Jucker; Nelson v. Bowler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence — attorney and engineering diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence under 35 U.S.C. 102(g) encompasses reasonable attorney-diligence and engineering-diligence and does not require abandoning all other work or responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable diligence means working reasonably hard on the application during the continuous critical period; reasonable backlog of unrelated cases handled expeditiously is acceptable. Case citations: Keizer v. Bradley; Emery v. Ronden; Bey v. Kollonitsch; Haskell v. Coleburne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical period for establishing diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a first conceiver who later reduces to practice, the critical diligence period begins just prior to the entry into the field of the party who was first to reduce to practice and continues until the first conceiver reduces to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry date of the first reducer depends on what that party relied upon (conception plus diligence, actual reduction, or constructive reduction). Case citations: Hull v. Davenport; Fritsch v. Lin; Rebstock v. Flouret; Justus v. Appenzeller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire diligence period must be accounted for by affirmative acts or acceptable excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must account for the entire period during which diligence is required by showing affirmative acts or acceptable excuses for any gaps; unexplained lapses (even short) can be fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bare statements of diligence are insufficient; examples show even 2-day or less-than-month gaps have been fatal. Acceptable excuses are narrowly construed (vacation for ill health may qualify; lack of funding or personnel typically does not). Case citations: Gould v. Schawlow; In re Harry; In re Mulder; Fitzgerald v. Arbib; Kendall v. Searles; Griffith v. Kanamaru; Litchfield v. Eigen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work relied upon to show diligence must be directly related to reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts or work used to demonstrate reasonable diligence must be directly related to reducing the invention in issue to practice; related but distinct activity is insufficient unless closely related inventions are properly connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under some circumstances work on closely related inventions can support diligence (Ginos v. Nedelec); however, fortuitous successes while working on different inventions do not show diligence toward the invention in issue. Case citations: Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; In re Jolley; Gunn v. Bosch; Broos v. Barton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in preparing and filing patent application credited to inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence of an attorney in preparing and filing a patent application can inure to the benefit of the inventor; conception may be established when a draft application is finished by counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney need not be flawless; reasonable diligence by counsel (including reasonable backlog and work on related cases contributing substantially) is acceptable. Short delays (e.g., six days to execute and file) have been held acceptable. Case citations: Haskell v. Coleburne; Bey v. Kollonitsch.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of diligence period marked by actual or constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The diligence period ends upon either an actual reduction to practice or a constructive reduction to practice (e.g., filing a patent application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is immaterial that the period ends by constructive rather than actual reduction to practice. Case citation: Justus v. Appenzeller.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 Obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability is not negated by the manner in which the invention was made. These are the baseline statutory criteria for obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) — Biotechnological process/composition special rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon timely election by the applicant, a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under section 102 and nonobvious under subsection (a) shall be considered nonobvious if (A) claims to the process and composition are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date, and (B) the composition and process were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent issues on the process, it must also contain claims to the composition used/made by that process or expire on the same date as the patent claiming the composition. The statute defines 'biotechnological process' to include (A) genetically altering or inducing organisms to express/alter nucleotide sequences or express specific physiological characteristics, (B) cell fusion producing cell lines expressing a specific protein, and (C) methods of using products produced by such processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — Common ownership/joint research agreement exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person that qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of 102 shall not preclude patentability where, at the time the claimed invention was made, the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this exception to apply the claimed invention must have been made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; the invention must result from activities within the scope of the agreement; and the patent application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. 'Joint research agreement' is defined as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
